beginner.name: Getting Started

beginner.nutrition: Apply the ½ veg – ¼ protein – ¼ carb plate for one meal per day
beginner.milestone: Complete 7/7 days; write 5 lines in a training journal each session

beginner.name: Building Base
beginner.desc: Keep week 1 structure but add slightly: +1 set or +5–10% reps.
beginner.focus: Squat to chair 3×10, knee push-up 3×10, cardio 30', technique micro-lesson
beginner.nutrition: Every main meal includes one protein source: eggs, fish, lean meat, beans
beginner.milestone: Plank 30 s unbroken; brisk walk 30' comfortably

beginner.name: Strengthening

beginner.focus: Goblet squat, standard push-up, band row, light RDL, plank 40 s

beginner.milestone: Squat 3×12 with good form; brisk walk 35' comfortably

beginner.name: Progressing
beginner.desc: Increase volume and intensity steadily; start tracking measurements.
beginner.focus: Goblet squat 3×12, push-up 3×10, dumbbell row, RDL, split squat
beginner.nutrition: Add more fibre, limit sugary drinks, drink enough water
beginner.milestone: Push-up 3×10 proper form; plank 45 s; brisk walk 40' Zone 2

beginner.name: Developing

busy.nutrition: Eat slowly, don't skip breakfast, stay hydrated

busy.name: More Efficient

busy.focus: Morning: push/pull/squat/core 10'. Lunch: brisk walk 5–10' if available

busy.name: Progressing

busy.name: Developing

busy.name: Mastery

beginner.detail: Squat, wall push-up, glute bridge, knee plank
details: Strength A covers 4 foundational movement patterns: squat (controlled sit-to-stand), wall push-up (safe for beginners), glute bridge (glute activation), and knee plank. Do 2–3 sets × 8–12 reps for each exercise.

Wall push-ups train the chest, front deltoid, and triceps at a gentle angle — ideal for building upper-body strength in weeks 1–4 without overloading. Once 3×15 feels easy, progress to an incline push-up off a table.
Rest 60 seconds between sets. In your first session, prioritise form over rep count. After 4 weeks, add 1 set or 2–3 reps once technique is consistent.

points.label: RPE 5–6 / 10
points.note: You can still hold a conversation

beginner.detail: Brisk walk 20–25', still able to speak short sentences
details: A brisk walk at Zone 2 intensity — you can say a short sentence but not hold a full conversation. This builds your aerobic base without taxing the muscles recovering from Monday's strength session.
Aim for 20–25 minutes at a pace that feels 'comfortably challenging'. If you can sing, speed up; if you can't say a word, slow down. Heart rate should sit around 60–70 % of your maximum.
Focus on posture: shoulders back, core lightly engaged, arms swinging naturally. Even a 20-minute walk done consistently beats sporadic longer sessions.

points.label: Outdoor preferred
points.note: Fresh air improves mood and adherence

beginner.detail: Hip hinge, towel row, split squat, dead bug
details: Strength B targets the posterior chain and balance: hip hinge (load the glutes/hamstrings instead of the back), towel row (upper-back at home), split squat (single-leg stability), and dead bug (anti-rotation core).
The hip hinge is critical for long-term back health. Practise 'pushing hips back toward the wall' as a cue. Once it clicks, the Romanian deadlift progression becomes safe and effective.
For the split squat, use a wall or chair for balance in the first weeks. Keep the front knee tracking over your second toe. Start with 8 reps per side, 2 sets.

points.label: Split squat balance
points.note: Use a wall if needed — no shame

points.label: Dead bug focus
points.note: Keep lower back flat on the floor

details: A 15–20 minute mobility session targeting areas most affected by strength training: hip flexors (tightened by sitting), hamstrings, chest and shoulder openers, and thoracic spine rotation.
Hold each stretch for 30–45 seconds and breathe into the tension rather than forcing the range. Mobility is a long-term investment — your squat depth and injury resilience depend on it.
Suggested flow: cat-cow 2 min → child's pose 1 min → pigeon stretch each side 2 min → doorway chest stretch 1 min → seated hamstring stretch 2 min → thoracic rotation 2 min.

beginner.detail: Sit-to-stand, glute bridge, bird-dog, calf raise
details: Strength C revisits Monday's patterns at lower volume and introduces bird-dog — an anti-extension core exercise that also trains coordination between opposite arm and leg.
Sit-to-stand builds functional leg strength from a chair, directly transferable to daily life. Focus on controlling the descent as much as the rise — the eccentric phase builds more strength.
Calf raises are often overlooked but crucial for ankle stability. Do them slowly: 2 seconds up, 1 second hold, 3 seconds down. 3×15 reps is sufficient.
A slightly longer walk than Tuesday — 25–30 minutes at a moderate pace. The goal is to accumulate aerobic volume without creating fatigue heading into the weekend.
Use this session to de-stress and reset mentally. Walking in natural light also helps regulate sleep-wake cycles, which directly improves recovery from strength training.
Optional: add 5 minutes of gentle bodyweight lunges or step-ups at the end to keep legs active. Skip if your legs feel heavy from the week.

points.label: Outdoor walking
points.note: Natural light boosts mood and sleep

points.label: Optional finish
points.note: 5 min gentle lunges if legs allow

details: Rest day is not wasted — it's when your body actually rebuilds. Gentle walking or stretching is fine. Avoid any intense exercise.
Take 5 minutes to write in your training journal: what felt good this week, what was hard, one thing to focus on next week. Research shows journalling triples habit retention.
Also review your sleep, hydration, and diet from the week. These three factors account for over 60 % of training results. Adjust anything clearly off before next week.

points.label: Hydration check
points.note: Did you hit 2 L this week?

busy.detail: Squat 30 s, push 30 s, glute bridge 30 s, plank 20 s × 2 rounds
details: Monday's 10-minute circuit: squat (lower body), push-up (upper push), glute bridge (posterior chain), and knee plank (core). Do 2 complete rounds with transitions under 10 seconds.
The goal is to move — imperfect but consistent. Even 10 minutes of circuit training done 5–6× per week produces measurable cardiovascular and strength improvements over 3 months.
Set a timer for 10 minutes and cycle through continuously. If you finish before the timer, start a 3rd round. Quality of movement matters more than speed.

busy.detail: Step touch 40 s + march in place 40 s × 3 rounds
details: Tuesday's low-impact cardio needs zero space and zero equipment. Step touch and marching in place keep the heart rate up without joint impact — ideal for tight schedules and indoor spaces.
3 rounds of 40 s step touch + 40 s march = roughly 4 minutes of continuous movement. Pair with 5 minutes of breathing and you have a complete 10-minute session.
If time allows, go for 4 rounds. Monitor your breathing: you should feel slightly winded but still able to say a word.

busy.detail: Dead bug 30 s, bird-dog 30 s, knee plank 20 s × 2 rounds
details: Wednesday is dedicated to core stability — the foundation of all movement. Dead bug trains anti-extension, bird-dog trains anti-rotation, and knee plank builds isometric endurance.
These exercises look simple but require real concentration. Keep your lower back flat and breathe throughout. Never hold your breath during planks.
2 rounds fit in 6–7 minutes. Add 2–3 minutes of neck and shoulder rolls to finish as a mini mobility break.

points.label: Plank 20 s
points.note: Quality over duration — no sagging hips

busy.detail: 10' full body: neck, shoulders, hips, hamstrings
details: Thursday is a 10-minute full-body mobility flow — the session purely dedicated to feeling better. Neck rolls, shoulder circles, hip circles, and a seated hamstring stretch form the sequence.
Mobility training reduces injury risk, improves posture (critical for desk workers), and speeds up recovery from the strength sessions earlier in the week.
Suggested flow: neck rolls 30 s each direction → shoulder circles 30 s → thoracic extension over a chair 1 min → hip circles 1 min each side → seated hamstring stretch 1 min each side.

points.label: Mindful movement
points.note: Slow and controlled — feel each joint

busy.detail: Squat, band row, glute bridge, wall push-up × 2 rounds
details: Friday's circuit mirrors Monday's but adds the band row — introducing a pulling pattern to balance the pushing done earlier. No resistance band? Substitute a towel-row using a door handle.
After a full week of short sessions, Friday might feel easier than expected. That's adaptation at work. If it genuinely feels too easy, add a 3rd round or slow each rep to a 2-second count.
Keep transitions between exercises under 10 seconds. The goal is keeping the heart rate elevated throughout the 10 minutes.
Saturday is an active recovery day — gentle enough to let your body repair but moving enough to keep the streak alive. A 10-minute brisk walk or a few flights of stairs is plenty.
Walking in natural light on Saturday morning helps reset the circadian rhythm, improving sleep quality going into Sunday. Even a walk to a local shop counts.
For stair climbing: aim for 4–6 flights at a relaxed pace. Monitor your breathing. This is restorative movement, not a workout.
Sunday is for nervous system recovery. Box breathing (4 s inhale → 4 s hold → 4 s exhale → 4 s hold) activates the parasympathetic system, reducing cortisol and improving sleep quality.
Follow with 5 minutes of journaling: one line about the week's wins, one about what was hard, one intention for next week. Brief reflective writing improves habit adherence and motivation.
Alternatively, use a guided meditation app for 5–10 minutes. The goal is mental rest — not more stimulus.

points.label: Journal 3 lines
points.note: Win · Hard · Intention for next week

fatloss.detail: Squat, push-up, band row, glute bridge, plank
details: Strength A is a 5-exercise full-body circuit that preserves and builds muscle while in a calorie deficit. Muscle mass is your metabolism — protect it with 3 strength sessions per week.
The band row is crucial here: most fat-loss programs over-emphasise push movements. The row counterbalances and supports good posture, which directly improves exercise performance.
Complete 3 sets × 10–12 reps per exercise. Rest 45–60 seconds. The moderate rest period keeps heart rate elevated while maintaining enough recovery for good technique.

points.label: Add weight gradually
points.note: Heavier = more fat burned at rest

fatloss.detail: Walk/cycling 30–35' Zone 2 — still able to talk
details: Zone 2 cardio (60–70 % max HR) is the most efficient fat-burning zone. At this intensity, your body preferentially uses fat as fuel rather than glycogen. It also creates very little recovery debt.
The talk test: you should be able to speak 4–5 words comfortably, but not sing. If you're gasping, slow down. If you're chatting freely, speed up slightly.
Walking briskly or cycling at 65–70 % effort for 30–35 minutes burns approximately 200–280 kcal and creates an ideal caloric deficit combined with your diet.

points.label: Fat-burning zone
points.note: 60–70 % max HR uses fat as fuel

fatloss.detail: Hip hinge, split squat, dead bug, calf raise
details: Strength B shifts focus to the posterior chain and single-leg movements: hip hinge (glutes/hamstrings), split squat (balance + leg strength), dead bug (core stability), and calf raise (ankle/lower-leg).
The hip hinge — done correctly — is one of the most effective movements for shaping the glutes and hamstrings while protecting the lower back. Cue: 'hinge at hips, push hips back, keep chest tall'.
Split squats expose bilateral strength imbalances that regular squats mask. Starting with the split squat ensures even leg development and reduces injury risk as training volume increases.

points.label: Hip hinge cue
points.note: Push hips back, chest tall, neutral back

fatloss.detail: Mobility 15' + target +2,000 extra steps in the day
details: NEAT (Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis) — all the movement you do outside structured workouts — accounts for 15–30 % of daily calorie burn. Adding 2,000 steps burns an extra 80–120 kcal.
Today's session starts with 15 minutes of mobility (hip flexors, hamstrings, thoracic spine). Then aim to add 2,000 extra steps throughout the day: take stairs, park farther away, walk during calls.
Tracking steps with a phone or watch makes NEAT measurable. Long-term, NEAT-active people burn 300–500 more kcal per day than sedentary peers of the same body size.

fatloss.detail: Push-up, scapular squeeze, glute bridge, bird-dog
details: Strength C introduces the scapular squeeze — a corrective exercise that counters the forward-rounded posture from desk work and helps the shoulder girdle function properly during pushing and rowing movements.
Glute bridge here serves as both a strength exercise and an active stretch for the hip flexors, which get tight from sitting. Focus on squeezing the glutes hard at the top of each rep.
3 sets × 12 reps. Shorter rest than Monday/Wednesday (40 s) to slightly elevate heart rate and increase caloric burn without sacrificing form quality.
Saturday's longer Zone 2 session is the weekly 'long slow distance' — a cardio term for sustained, moderate-intensity work that trains the aerobic system and burns significant calories.
At 35–45 minutes, this session burns 250–350 kcal. Combine with a 200–300 kcal daily food deficit and you have a weekly deficit of approximately 3,000 kcal — roughly 0.4 kg of fat per week.
Listen to your body: if your legs feel tired from Friday's strength session, walk at an easy pace. If you feel fresh, push the pace slightly. Recovery is as important as effort.

points.label: 250–350 kcal burned
points.note: Biggest calorie session of the week

points.label: 35–45 min
points.note: Zone 2 — brisk walk or easy cycling

points.label: Listen to your body
points.note: Tired from Friday? Go easy today

points.label: Weekly deficit
points.note: ~0.4 kg fat loss per week when combined

fatloss.detail: Light walk 20' + review weight & waist measurements
details: Sunday is active recovery and data day. A 20-minute easy walk at a conversational pace helps clear lactate, reduces muscle soreness, and keeps the movement habit intact.
After the walk, take your weekly weight and waist measurement. Do this at the same time (ideally morning, after the bathroom). Trend over 4 weeks matters more than any single measurement.

If the scale went up, don't panic — water retention from increased training and carbs is normal. Track the 4-week moving average instead. Waist circumference is often the more reliable fat-loss indicator.

points.label: Morning weigh-in
points.note: Same time, same conditions every Sunday

points.label: 4-week trend
points.note: One number means nothing — trend matters

muscle.detail: Bench/push-up, row, OHP, lat pulldown, curl
details: Upper A is a horizontal push + pull session: bench press or push-up (horizontal push), row (horizontal pull), overhead press (vertical push), lat pulldown (vertical pull), and bicep curl (arm isolation).
Always pair push and pull within the same session to maintain shoulder balance. If you only push without pulling, the anterior deltoid and pec minor shorten over time, causing shoulder impingement.
Complete 3 sets × 8–10 reps for compound movements (bench, row, OHP, lat pulldown), 3×12 for the curl. Rest 90 seconds between compound sets.

points.label: Push-pull balance
points.note: Every push needs an equal pull

points.label: Compound priority
points.note: Bench, row, OHP, lat pulldown first

muscle.detail: Squat, Romanian deadlift, leg press, calf, plank
details: Lower A is quad-dominant: squat (primary quad driver), Romanian deadlift (hip hinge and hamstring), leg press (quad volume), calf raise (lower leg), and plank (core stability between sets).
The squat and RDL are complementary — squat loads the knee joint and quad, while RDL loads the hip joint and hamstring. Together they give complete lower-body development without imbalances.
Start with 4 sets × 6–8 reps for squats at RPE 7. Add the RDL at 3×8–10. Finish with leg press 3×12 and calves 3×15. Plank 30–45 s between sets when resting.
Wednesday is active recovery between two heavy lower-body days. A 25–30 minute walk at Zone 1–2 intensity flushes metabolic waste products from Monday and Tuesday, reducing next-day soreness.
Follow the walk with a 10-minute full-body stretching sequence, focusing on the hip flexors, hamstrings, and chest and shoulder areas stressed during the first two days.
This session also functions as a mental reset mid-week. The combination of light movement and stretching has been shown to reduce training fatigue and improve sleep quality.

muscle.detail: Incline press, pull-up/lat, lateral raise, tricep
details: Upper B shifts emphasis to the upper chest (incline press), upper back and lats (pull-up or lat pulldown), and shoulder and arm accessories (lateral raise, tricep extension).
Incline press at 30–45 degrees targets the clavicular head of the pec, which often lags behind the sternal head trained in flat bench. This creates a fuller, more complete chest.
Lateral raises are the primary exercise for creating shoulder width. Use a weight you can control for a full 3-second negative. Swinging and using momentum defeats the purpose.

points.label: Pull-up priority
points.note: Or lat pulldown if not there yet

muscle.detail: Deadlift, hip thrust, walking lunge, core
details: Lower B is hip-dominant and targets the glutes, hamstrings, and lower back: deadlift (full posterior chain), hip thrust (direct glute isolation), walking lunge (leg and balance), and core finisher.
The conventional deadlift is the king of posterior chain exercises. Key cues: bar close to shins, hips hinge back, chest tall, push floor away — don't pull the bar up. This is a push, not a pull.
Hip thrust with a barbell or dumbbell directly loads the glutes through full hip extension — something squats and deadlifts can't fully achieve. 3×10–12 with a 2-second squeeze at the top.

points.label: Deadlift is king
points.note: Push floor away — don't yank the bar

points.label: Hip thrust isolation
points.note: 2-second squeeze at top — feel the glutes

muscle.detail: Squat, push, row, plank — RPE 6, form focus
details: Saturday's light full-body session maintains movement patterns at low intensity (RPE 6 — 4 reps left in tank). This is not a workout to build muscle — it's a session to stay active and reinforce technique.
Use this session to work on weak points in technique you noticed earlier in the week. Slow each rep down to 3 seconds on the negative phase. Record yourself if possible.
No need to add weight. The goal is movement quality and active recovery. Finish in 25–30 minutes maximum.

points.label: Film your form
points.note: Saturday is the ideal technique check day

points.label: 25–30 min max
points.note: Finish early — don't turn it into a full session

points.label: Technique focus
points.note: Fix what was off earlier this week

details: Sunday is genuine rest. If you feel recovered and energised, do 10–15 minutes of mobility work (hip circles, shoulder circles, pigeon pose, hamstring stretch). If you feel tired, rest completely.
Overtraining is real. After 5–6 days of structured training, the body needs 24–48 hours without significant stress to consolidate the adaptations from the week.
Use Sunday to plan next week's sessions, ensure recovery nutrition (protein + carbs), and review your progress log. Long-term success depends on sustainable rhythms, not heroic weekly efforts.

points.label: 10–15 min mobility
points.note: If you feel good — not if you're tired

details: Monday's Zone 2 session is the cornerstone of endurance training. Zone 2 (60–70 % max HR) develops mitochondrial density in slow-twitch muscle fibres — the engine of aerobic performance.
After 30 minutes of Zone 2 cardio, add 5 minutes of core work: plank, dead bug, or bird-dog. Core strength is underrated in endurance sports — it holds your running and cycling posture when tired.
The talk test: you should be able to speak in short sentences but not comfortably carry on a long conversation. Heart rate monitor or RPE 5–6 works equally well.

points.label: +5 min core
points.note: Holds form when you're tired in a race

points.label: Cornerstone session
points.note: The most important workout of the week

endurance.detail: Squat, push-up, band row, glute bridge 3×10
details: Tuesday's minimal strength session takes just 20–25 minutes and prevents the muscle loss that often accompanies high-cardio training plans. Muscle loss slows metabolism and reduces running economy.
3 sets × 10 reps of squat, push-up, band row, and glute bridge covers all major movement patterns. These are maintenance sets, not growth sets — keep weight moderate and don't train to failure.
This session also doubles as an active recovery from Monday's cardio. Keep intensity low (RPE 6), rest 45–60 seconds between sets, and finish with 5 minutes of light stretching.

points.label: Muscle maintenance
points.note: Prevents muscle loss on high cardio plans

points.label: Running economy
points.note: Stronger muscles = better form at mile 8

details: Wednesday's interval session is where aerobic fitness gains accelerate. After a 5-minute easy warm-up, complete 5 rounds of 2 minutes at high intensity (Zone 4–5, RPE 8) alternated with 2 minutes easy.
Zone 4–5 intervals develop VO2max — the maximum amount of oxygen your body can use during exercise. A higher VO2max means faster sustainable paces at all distances.
Cool down with 5 minutes at an easy pace. Total session: approximately 30 minutes. Perceived exertion during the hard intervals should be 8–9/10 — genuinely uncomfortable.

points.label: VO2max builder
points.note: Fastest way to improve aerobic capacity

points.label: 5 min cool-down
points.note: Never stop abruptly after high intensity

details: Thursday is a complete rest from cardiovascular work. The 15–20 minute mobility session focuses on the areas most stressed by endurance training: hip flexors, IT band (lateral thigh), hamstrings, and thoracic spine.
Endurance athletes often develop stiffness in the hip flexors (shortened by cycling) and hamstrings (tightened by running). Regular mobility work prevents these imbalances from becoming injuries.
Suggested sequence: neck rolls 1 min → chest opener 1 min → cat-cow 2 min → hip flexor lunge stretch 2 min each side → IT band foam roll 2 min each side → seated hamstring stretch 2 min each side.

points.label: Injury prevention
points.note: Flexibility gaps become injuries at high volume

endurance.detail: Split squat, RDL, bird-dog, plank, calf raise
details: Friday's strength session adds single-leg exercises (split squat, Romanian deadlift) that directly translate to running efficiency. Single-leg strength prevents the compensatory patterns that cause most running injuries.

Bird-dog and plank maintain the core stability needed to hold form during long efforts. Research shows that runners with strong cores maintain stride efficiency for longer, delaying the point where form breaks down.
Keep intensity low-moderate (RPE 6–7). This is a support session for your endurance training, not the star of the show. 3×10 per exercise, rest 45 seconds.

points.label: RPE 6–7 only
points.note: Support session — not the main event

points.label: Calf raise essential
points.note: Calves take 6× bodyweight per step running

details: Saturday's long session is the weekly anchor of endurance training. Going from 30 minutes on Monday to 45–60 minutes today progressively builds aerobic base without overtraining.

Maintain strict Zone 2: if your pace naturally feels easy, resist the urge to push harder. The goal is fat oxidation adaptation — the ability to use fat as fuel efficiently, which protects glycogen stores in long events.
Bring water for sessions over 45 minutes. For cycling, a light snack is optional but not required at this duration. Focus on smooth, consistent effort throughout.

points.label: Fat oxidation
points.note: Teach body to burn fat, spare glycogen

points.label: Bring water
points.note: Hydrate every 15 min — don't wait to feel thirsty

points.label: Stay in Zone 2
points.note: Resist urge to push harder — trust the process

endurance.detail: Light walk 20–30' or full rest if fatigued
details: Sunday is recovery. The decision between a light walk and complete rest should be guided by how you feel: slight fatigue = easy walk; significant fatigue or soreness = complete rest. Never push through real fatigue.

A 20–30 minute easy walk at Zone 1 (fully conversational) promotes blood flow without creating training stress. This is often called 'active recovery' and is preferred over complete inactivity for most athletes.
Use Sunday to refuel with quality food: protein + carbohydrates to replenish glycogen and support muscle repair. Good Sunday nutrition directly improves Monday's performance.
Monday is the heaviest tri-modal day: cycling builds aerobic base, upper-body gym work maintains strength, and swimming develops technique and shoulder endurance. Total training volume: ~2 hours.
Cycling first while fresh to get quality Zone 2–3 effort. Gym upper-body at moderate intensity (RPE 7) — push-up/bench, row, OHP, lat pulldown. Swim last as the aerobic finisher.
Sequence matters: cycling before gym to avoid pre-fatiguing the legs for lower-body gym days later in the week. Total calorie burn for the day: approximately 700–900 kcal.

points.label: Cycling first
points.note: Fresh legs for quality Zone 2–3 output

points.label: ~700–900 kcal
points.note: Fuel well: carbs before + protein after

advanced.detail: Gym Lower 45' (Squat, RDL, Leg press) + Swim 50'
details: Tuesday focuses on lower-body strength + swimming. Lower-body gym work is done at full intensity (RPE 8) since cycling is off today. Squat 4×6, RDL 3×8, leg press 3×10 as the main compound lifts.
Swimming after lower-body gym uses the upper body and cardiovascular system with legs already pre-fatigued. This trains swimming technique under fatigue — valuable race-day simulation.
Prioritise 1,500–2,000 m of total swimming. Focus on stroke efficiency, not speed. Pull buoy sets are useful to isolate the upper body if legs feel very tired.

points.label: Full leg effort
points.note: RPE 8 — no cycling today so push legs

points.label: Pull buoy option
points.note: Isolate upper body if legs are spent

details: Wednesday mirrors Monday but with a push-focused gym session (bench/push-up, OHP, dips, tricep) instead of full upper body. This allows for higher specificity and slightly more volume on pushing muscles.
Cycling at Zone 2–3 (40 minutes) maintains aerobic volume mid-week. Push gym session at RPE 7 — not maximal, as the goal is training volume accumulation, not peak strength output.
Swimming completes the tri-modal day. Focus on freestyle technique: hand entry in line with shoulder, full arm extension, hip rotation. Quality of stroke beats raw distance at this stage.

points.label: Technique swim
points.note: Hand entry, hip rotation, full extension

advanced.detail: Gym Pull 45' (Deadlift, row, face pull) + Swim 50'
details: Thursday is pull-focused strength + swimming. Deadlift (4×6, RPE 8) as the primary compound movement, followed by horizontal row (3×10) and face pull (3×15 for shoulder health).

The face pull is non-negotiable for advanced athletes doing heavy push volume: it trains the posterior deltoid and external rotators, preventing the shoulder impingement that sidelines many high-volume trainers.
Swimming after the pull session naturally continues the rowing pattern in water, training the lats, rhomboids, and biceps through a different range of motion. Total volume: 1,500–2,000 m.

points.label: Face pull essential
points.note: Prevents shoulder impingement at high volume

points.label: Lats in water
points.note: Row → swim: same muscles, different plane

points.label: Push-pull balance
points.note: Week total: equal push and pull volume

details: Friday's session is full tri-modal: cycling + full-body gym + swim. The full-body gym session (30 minutes) at low intensity (RPE 6) reinforces movement patterns without creating significant fatigue heading into Saturday's long ride.

Full-body gym at RPE 6 means: squat, push, row, plank — all at about 60 % of maximum effort. This is technique maintenance, not strength building. Use the session to refine any weak points noticed earlier in the week.
Friday's swim should be relaxed (Zone 1–2). The goal is to stay aerobically active, maintain swim feel in the water, and prepare psychologically for Saturday's long effort.

points.label: Zone 2 cycling
points.note: Active prep for Saturday's long ride

details: Saturday's long ride is the weekly peak training stimulus. 90–120 minutes in Zone 2 (65–70 % max HR) builds maximal aerobic base, fat oxidation capacity, and mental endurance.
Fuel during the ride: for sessions over 75 minutes, consume 30–40 g of fast carbohydrates every 30–40 minutes (banana, energy bar, rice cake). Hydrate with 500–750 ml per hour.

After the ride, spend 20 minutes on mobility: hip flexors (tightened by cycling position), thoracic spine (hunched over handlebars), and hamstrings. This recovery work prevents cumulative stiffness over the training cycle.

Sunday's recovery ride is one of the most important sessions of the week. Zone 1–2 cycling (55–65 % max HR) flushes lactate from Saturday's long effort, reduces muscle soreness, and maintains training frequency without adding stress.
This is the session where athletes make the most mistakes: going too hard because they feel good after Saturday's rest. Zone 1–2 means you should be able to comfortably read a book while pedalling.
After the ride, prioritise nutrition (protein + complex carbohydrates), hydration, and sleep preparation. The adaptations from a week of training are consolidated during Sunday night's sleep.

points.label: Zone 1–2 only
points.note: If you're breathing hard — slow down

points.label: Sleep 8+ h tonight
points.note: Where this week's gains are consolidated

ui.progress_note: Increase gradually each week; listen to your body
ui.if_achieve_early: If you hit the milestone before week {{week}}, increase intensity or add new exercises.
ui.progress_eval: Evaluate progress every 2 weeks: compare form, completion time, and how your endurance feels.
ui.water_note: Drink 2–2.5 litres of water daily; prioritise plain water and fresh vegetable juices.
ui.meal_timing_note: Eat 3 full meals; limit unhealthy snacks, especially after 8 pm.
ui.plate_note: ½ veg – ¼ protein – ¼ carb
ui.complete_note: Tick each day on the calendar
ui.reward_note: Treat yourself when you hit a milestone
